newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia congratulates Britain's Blair, HK unmoved.
newsitem.headline: Asia congratulates Britain's Blair, HK unmoved.

text.p: Asian nations on Friday congratulated Britain's Labour Party on its landslide election win, but leaders in the British colony of Hong Kong were unmoved and instead turned their focus to their future master -- China.
Tony Blair's new-look Labour Party swept back to power on Friday for the first time since 1979 in its biggest-ever victory, inflicting a humiliating defeat on John Major's Conservatives.
In Australia, the nation's opposition Labor Party cheered Blair's win and said his success was in part a result of the lessons he learned from the Australian Labor Party.
Conservative Prime Minister John Howard also congratulated Blair, but said his counterpart John Major never stood a chance.
Malaysia said it looked forward to continuing its "excellent relations" with Britain, despite past trade disputes, while Bangladesh said it expected stronger ties.
In Tokyo, the only immediate reaction was to sell sterling, which fell across the board in late trade partly in reaction to fears the Labour Party would like to take a soft sterling policy.
The currency fell below $1.62 after stop-loss sales were triggered near that level, but support was seen around $1.6150 on commercial buying interest.
Hong Kong's political leaders, businessmen and activists failed to see what the fuss was about and said Britain's political scene was now largely irrelevant to the territory's future.
British influence is rapidly fading in Hong Kong, with only 60 days to go before the handover of sovereignty after 156 years of colonial rule.

The last British Governor Chris Patten and the territory's future leader Tung Chee-hwa congratulated Labour Party leader Tony Blair on his victory. Tung said he looked forward to working with Labour, while Patten stressed the importance of bipartisan support for policies on Hong Kong.
Patten, the mastermind of John Major's victory in the 1992 British election, was playing tennis when he heard of Major's defeat on Friday. "Oh No!" Patten gasped.
But it was not clear if it was the poll results or his tennis game that upset the man tipped as a possible new Tory party leader.
"I don't think we are disappointed or elated, either way," said Henry Tang, head of the Hong Kong Federation of Industry.

"It's far more important for Hong Kong in economic terms and in political terms for our new government to be on good terms with the United States than with Great Britain," said Ted Thomas, founder of a campaign to boost Hong Kong's image abroad.

Malaysia's Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Kuala Lumpur "congratulates Tony Blair as the new prime minister and believe we will continue the excellent relations between Britain and Malaysia".

Bangladesh's State Minister for Foreign Affairs Abul Hasan Chowdhury said he looked confidently towards a strengthening of the existing good relations and more meaningful cooperation with London in future.

Australia's Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley said Blair's victory was a result of his ability to restructure the British Labour Party to make it relevant to the British people after a long period in opposition.
"And he learned a lot from us, as he would acknowledge himself...," said Beazley.
Australia's Labor government was thrown out of office in 1996 in a landslide similar to that which has brought Labour into power in Britain.
